policy: Architecture, comparison, responsibility-boundary, and teaching mental-model diagrams migrate only after the deterministic Excalidraw pipeline exists.

items.claim: The four accelerators differ mainly in who schedules a tile and how the tile moves between compute and memory resources.
items.question: How does one tile progress through each accelerator execution model?
items.audience: Readers entering the cross-architecture learning path
items.scope: One aligned overview of NVIDIA GPU, Groq TSP, Tenstorrent Tensix, and Google TPU; no microarchitectural detail
items.readingOrder: Left-to-right aligned small multiples using the same comparison axes

items.claim: Compilation, host runtime, device execution, and scale-out coordination are separate responsibility boundaries rather than one monolithic runtime.
items.question: Which layer owns each decision between a model and multi-LPU execution?
items.audience: Readers building a public-evidence mental model of the Groq inference stack
items.scope: Framework through scale-out responsibilities; excludes undocumented commercial API details
items.readingOrder: Top-to-bottom layers with explicit compile-time and run-time boundaries

items.claim: Dynamo orchestrates a repeated GPU-attention and LPX-FFN activation loop rather than moving an arbitrary CUDA kernel to the LPU.
items.question: What crosses the GPU-LPX boundary during one decode token?
items.scope: AFD request path and intermediate activations; excludes unpublished transport and fusion details
items.readingOrder: Request routing into prefill, then a highlighted decode loop, then token output

items.claim: Reader, compute, and writer kernels overlap by exchanging tile ownership through circular buffers in local SRAM.
items.question: Who moves, computes, and releases each tile in a Tensix core pipeline?
items.audience: TT-Metalium learners and cross-architecture performance engineers
items.scope: Per-core steady-state pipeline; excludes the complete device and mesh topology
items.readingOrder: Three responsibility lanes around input and output circular-buffer ownership

items.claim: A GPU SM keeps more dynamic scheduling and thread state in hardware, while Tensix shifts more placement, data movement, and buffering responsibility to software-visible dataflow mechanisms.
items.question: Which responsibilities are implemented differently by an NVIDIA SM and a Tensix core?
items.audience: GPU developers learning the Tensix execution contract
items.scope: Responsibility comparison, not a throughput or feature-equivalence chart
items.readingOrder: Two aligned small multiples with matched scheduling, compute, memory, and movement rows
